entry.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
entry.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

entry.title: Mixed Engression: Distributional Regression for Multivariate Mixed-Type Responses
entry.summary: Estimating the conditional distribution of multivariate responses with continuous and binary components requires capturing their dependence, respecting their different supports, and accommodating potentially heavy-tailed continuous outcomes. We propose mixed engression, which fits a continuous generator using energy losses induced by bounded discrepancies and then thresholds its soft binary outputs to produce mixed-response samples. Because the discrepancies are bounded, the population objective remains well defined without response-moment assumptions. However, we show that the full-response energy distance for the complete response vector can tend to zero before thresholding yet remain bounded away from zero afterward as response dimensions grow. A separate energy loss on the entire binary vector captures discrepancies obscured by the full-response comparison and controls the effect of thresholding. The generator is therefore fitted using an augmented energy loss that combines the full-response and binary components. Under compositional smoothness of the structural functions and a uniform threshold-margin condition, we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the final sampler's full-response error for sparse ReLU estimators of models driven by Gaussian or Student-t structural noise, yielding polynomial convergence rates up to logarithmic factors. We also establish consistency when the covariate, response, and noise dimensions grow under suitable conditions. Simulations show improved accuracy relative to the comparison methods under the full-response energy distance, including in heavy-tailed settings. Moderate binary augmentation substantially improves binary-distribution accuracy while largely preserving full-response accuracy.

entry.title: Neural LoFi with Backward Coupling: A Spectral Theory of Cross-Layer Feature Learning
entry.summary: During joint training, backpropagation allows later layers to reshape earlier representations, a feedback mechanism absent from purely layer-wise learning. We extend Neural Low-Degree Filtering (Neural LoFi), a recently proposed layer-wise spectral surrogate for feature learning, to capture this interaction. Starting from the exact backpropagation gradients, we derive a local coupling between a neuron's incoming weights and its corresponding next-layer column. In a controlled small-initialization regime with smooth activations and fixed surroundings, these dynamics amplify singular modes of a cross-layer correlation operator. Each growing mode pairs an earlier feature with an upper-layer response through shared neuron coefficients. This motivates a backward-coupling algorithm in which upper-layer sensitivities generate sample-dependent effective labels for earlier spectral steps, while corrected features refine upward transmission. A function-space variational principle characterizes the selected feature-response pairs by maximizing the label correlation of their product under kernel-norm constraints. For three-layer networks, we derive self-consistent continuous-time dynamics for the filtered hidden-layer features, the activation kernels, and the network output under the proposed backward coupling. In a hierarchical multi-index model, we establish a feature-recovery separation: backward coupling recovers lower-layer directions invisible to the original forward label-weighted statistic. The linear specialization recovers residual-dependent singular-mode dynamics, while paired modes provide a dynamical mechanism for linked low-rank covariance components consistent with the rainbow-network picture. Experiments with fully connected and convolutional networks on binary CIFAR-10 show improved accuracy over forward Neural LoFi at matched widths.

entry.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
entry.summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

entry.title: Structure and Exact Certification of Nonnegative Tensor Decompositions
entry.summary: We study the structure and exact certification of nonnegative tensor decompositions supplied through rational factor matrices. Every failure of minimality or essential uniqueness contains an irreducible positive exchange between $p$ supplied terms and $q$ competing terms. A dimension count based on the Lovitz--Petrov splitting theorem bounds the effective order of such an exchange, the sum over the modes of the joint factor-span dimension minus one, by $p+q-2$, and this bound is attained at every supplied length $R\ge2$. After eliminating ambient-row variables by the Farkas lemma, the resulting semialgebraic systems have fewer than $2R^2$ real variables. For input bit length $L$, this gives a deterministic $G(R)L^{O(R^2)}$-time algorithm that computes the nonnegative rank and an exact minimum-length decomposition, decides minimality and essential uniqueness, and returns exact witnesses when either property fails. The exponent is independent of the tensor order and the mode dimensions. For Lebesgue moment tensors, positive quadrature determines the nonnegative rank and the uniqueness behavior, and some rational length-$R$ inputs force a common field of degree at least $\lfloor R/2\rfloor!$ for any exact minimum-length output. As an illustration, an implementation resolves all 114 instances left inconclusive by earlier positive-scattering criteria, of which 95 are minimal and essentially unique and 19 are minimal but nonunique.

entry.title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes
entry.summary: There is growing evidence that the performance of a neural network depends largely on a small subset of its weights, which are typically identified by training a dense network and pruning it afterwards. Within a Bayesian framework, pruning can be directly incorporated through a spike-and-slab prior, providing a proper treatment of the uncertainties involved, both with respect to pruning and to parameter uncertainty. In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), sampling by MCMC is notoriously hard. We demonstrate that modern Monte Carlo methods based on piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) can be used to sample posteriors of BNNs asymptotically exact whenever numerically constructed rate bounds hold. Spike-and-slab priors can be incorporated through sticky versions of the PDMPs, setting weights exactly to zero during sampling. We examine the predictive performance and convergence of the samplers, and show that sparse BNNs sampled this way can be more robust to input noise than dense ones.

entry.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs
entry.summary: We study strongly adaptive regret for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, a setting that evaluates a learner's performance over arbitrary sub-intervals. This framework captures complex sequential decision-making problems where both the environment and the cost of switching decisions fluctuate over time. We propose a novel algorithm which, for any interval $[a,b] \subseteq [T]$, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(\|g_t\|^2+λ_t\|g_t\|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $λ_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round $t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of this development, we further establish the first strongly-adaptive guarantees under delayed feedback. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.

entry.title: Score-Preserving Continual Lasso under Task Shift
entry.summary: Continual learning (CL) aims to learn from sequential tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting when historical data are no longer accessible. We study continual learning for high-dimensional sparse linear regression, where $\ell_1$ regularization creates a difficulty absent from continual ridge regression: that recursively reusing an $\ell_1$-penalized estimator can propagate earlier shrinkage and accumulate regularization bias across tasks. We propose score-preserving continual Lasso (SP-CL), which separates sparse estimation from state transmission by preserving the historical squared-loss score. Under squared loss, its cumulative estimator exactly recovers a full-history Lasso minimizer. When task coefficients coincide, it inherits the full-history sparse rate. For related task-specific coefficients, SP-CL uses a regularized current-task correction that leaves the transmitted state unchanged and attains the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition. We also derive Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions that distinguish historical information loss, task conflict, and current-task specialization, and validate the resulting regimes in simulation.

entry.title: Acquisition for Spherical-Linear Bayesian Optimization on the Cube
entry.summary: Recent work demonstrated that executing Bayesian Optimization (BO) using simply a linear surrogate with a clever transformation is enough to approximate the performance of the standard Gaussian-Process (GP) based version on high-dimensional test functions. When the decision region is a sphere, this strategy admits rapid exact acquisition. However, it is the unit cube we encounter most often in the BO literature, and in this setting a standard approach, namely a multi-start quasi-Newton method, is employed for solving the acquisition subproblem. In this article, we will discuss a series of results, both positive and negative, regarding the complexity of global resolution of various acquisition subproblems over the unit cube. On the basis of this discussion, we will propose a new acquisition function which is globally optimizable using significantly less execution time than the incumbent approach while maintaining or improving performance. The resulting method is competitive with GP-based BO in terms of accuracy per evaluation, and is superior in terms of accuracy per walltime on black-boxes of low to moderate computational intensity.

entry.title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
entry.summary: Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

entry.title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
entry.summary: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.

entry.title: Exact Global Minimax Risk near Nonidentification
entry.summary: We study squared-error estimation when a nuisance parameter is unidentified on a submodel but affects a target that vanishes there. For models with higher-order profile expansions, we give sufficient conditions under which the largest critical-path minimax risk is the exact asymptotic minimax risk over the full parameter space. An efficient observable feature, negligible calibration error and stable recovery yield one estimator attaining the leading constant uniformly, with the profile coordinates unknown. The estimator uses calibration estimates, a local feature mean and an empirical recovery feature. The constant is expressed through a bounded-normal decision problem. We verify the conditions in two models. In centered Gaussian logistic errors-in-variables regression with one surrogate and two unknown variances, we determine the fifth-order global coefficient risk and its exact constant. A sparse extension separates variance-decomposition uncertainty from direction estimation and specifies when the scalar constant is preserved. In a degree-balanced replicated-network model, we determine the sixth-order global edge-contrast risk when block proportions are unknown. Triangles identify a parameter combination; a bowtie supplies the additional information needed for the contrast.

entry.title: Random Jump Forests
entry.summary: Random jump forests are introduced as a nonparametric tool for estimating conditional cumulative transition rates and occupation probabilities in multi-state models. The main idea is that a single tree partitions the covariate space for all transitions simultaneously, using partially observed trajectories, and with Nelson--Aalen estimators at the terminal nodes. Occupation probabilities are recovered through the product integral without requiring the Markov assumption. Uniform consistency and a functional central limit theorem for the estimators of cumulative rates can be established under the assumption that the covariate vector takes finitely many values, and under suitable splitting conditions. In particular, pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands are available in the Markov case. Simulation studies show a predictive accuracy close to the correctly specified benchmark models and marked improvements when benchmarks are misspecified, with further illustration on four biomedical data sets. In the coverage study, confidence bands attain near-nominal coverage in several settings, with pooling of heterogeneous rates being the main source of possible undercoverage. The method, including prediction assessment and variable importance, is implemented in the R package JumpForests.

entry.title: Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning
entry.summary: Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network. This work proposes a C++17 processing pipeline applied to the Tour Perret LoRaWAN dataset (421 937 frames, June 2021--June 2023, 5 devices). A systematic coverage audit integrated into the extraction phase reveals that CO2 is completely missing (0% coverage) and pressure is reported only by an isolated base module (Wyres, 4.24% of the corpus), invalidating the initial hypothesis of a joint four-variable analysis. The analysis is refocused on the Temperature--Humidity pair, jointly available across 205{,}005 frames (95.76%) from 4 Elsys EMS sensors. The pipeline sequentially performs anomaly detection (modified Z-score, Isolation Forest), bivariate Principal Component Analysis, clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and a multilayer perceptron predicting humidity from temperature and time, whose residuals serve as a detector for slow drift. On real-world data: Temperature--Humidity correlation r=-0.662, two-component PCA (PC1 =83.1% of variance), Isolation Forest detects 2.12% multivariate anomalies while univariate Z-score detects none, calibrated DBSCAN isolates 0.17% noise across 13 clusters, and the MLP achieves $R^2=0.672$ (RMSE =10.54%) in cross-validation. This work demonstrates that per-variable coverage auditing prior to modeling is a necessary methodological step for heterogeneous multi-sensor IoT datasets.

entry.title: Optimal Multiclass Online Regret with Arbitrary Label Spaces
entry.summary: We determine the optimal regret in agnostic multiclass online learning with arbitrary, possibly infinite, label spaces. For every hypothesis class of multiclass Littlestone dimension $d<\infty$, we prove a regret upper bound of $O(\min\{T,\sqrt{dT}\})$ over $T$ rounds, matching the known lower bound. This resolves a question of Hanneke et al. (2023) and extends the optimal binary regret bound of Alon et al. (2021). Our proof strengthens the one-sided expert cover of Hanneke et al. (2023) to a fractional cover. We combine this cover with a minimax reduction to a finite expert game, whose best-response rewards provide the disagreement bounds needed for chaining.

entry.title: Empirical concentration for chains with infinite memory
entry.summary: Concentration inequalities for time series usually involve unknown quantities measuring dependence. This prevents their direct use as confidence bounds, or as criteria for learning algorithms. Recent works proved empirical concentration inequalities for stationary Markov chains, where the unknown quantities are estimated. We extend this approach beyond the Markov case, by considering stationary chains with infinite memory. We first establish a bounded-differences inequality on bounded Polish metric spaces under a summable Wasserstein contraction condition. We then estimate its dependence coefficients from a single trajectory, using either transition counts when the state space is finite, or derivatives of kernel conditional-density estimates for a continuous state space. We give general error bounds and illustrate their dependence on the memory tail. Finally, a fixed multiplicative safety factor turns these estimators into empirical concentration bounds. While some regularity assumptions are required to make the bounds empirical, our procedure remains fully adaptive in the sense that it does not require the knowledge of the constants involved in these assumptions. The empirical confidence bounds derived from our results are asymptotically as tight as the theoretical ones.

entry.title: Federated Nonparametric Regression with Heterogeneous Clients
entry.summary: Whether a federated predictor benefits an individual client depends on both population heterogeneity and estimation uncertainty. We study this question for Nadaraya--Watson regression in a triangular array with potentially different fitting and evaluation distributions. Each client transmits local kernel summaries, allowing the server to construct a covariate-density-weighted federated estimator without centralizing individual observations. A client combines its fitted local predictor with the federated predictor through a prescribed weight, and gain is the paired reduction in squared prediction loss on an independent audit observation. Exact identities characterize both the gain of the realized fitted pair and its repeated-fitting mean. We also establish pointwise inference for the federated estimator. A two-stage analysis of client gains separates fitting variability from audit variability, retains the covariance created when a client's observations enter both its local estimator and the common server estimator, and yields fixed-block simultaneous inference across clients. Robustness is examined under two perturbation models. A Kullback--Leibler neighborhood provides a variance-sensitive lower certificate in a regular positive-gain-variance regime, while an $L_2$ neighborhood yields an exact least-favorable regression direction and robust value. Exact-model, vanishing-variance, and exact-zero-direction boundaries are kept separate because their scalar inputs are nonregular. The framework thus distinguishes decisions about a realized fitted pair from claims about the learning procedure under repeated fitting.

entry.title: Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport
entry.summary: Background-error covariance models are central to atmospheric data assimilation because they spread partial observational information across space, variables, and dynamically coupled scales. Ensemble and variational methods exploit this covariance geometry efficiently, but their standard analysis formulations are largely built around Gaussian or locally quadratic approximations. Score-based ensemble filtering provides a framework for nonlinear distributional transport, but existing Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) formulations lack an intrinsic covariance-mediated pathway for propagating likelihood information from observed to unobserved state components. We introduce a covariance-informed ensemble score filter (CI-EnSF) that embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry directly into the forward diffusion and reverse transport. The proposed forward diffusion is covariance-shaped in standardized state space and becomes isotropic under the corresponding control-variable transformation. This covariance structure continuously propagates observational information from observed to unobserved state components throughout the reverse transport analysis trajectory. Experiments with Lorenz-96 and surface quasi-geostrophic (SQG) dynamics show a clear regime dependence. For linear observations, a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate, while CI-EnSF maintains stable cycling and effective covariance-mediated information propagation. Under strongly nonlinear observations and under climatological initialization, CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness than Gaussian ensemble benchmarks such as the LETKF, with improvements extending across spatial scales in the nonlinear SQG experiment. These results suggest that the principal benefit of CI-EnSF arises from combining nonlinear distributional transport with the mature covariance geometry used in conventional data assimilation.

entry.title: Implicit Neural Representations for Variational Problems on Graphons
entry.summary: We propose a neural exploratory framework for variational problems over graphons, i.e., symmetric measurable functions $[0,1]^2 \to [0,1]$, that arise as limits of dense graph sequences. Such problems are central to two parts of the mathematical literature: extremal graph theory, which studies graph parameter optimisation under given restrictions, often for those graphs with a large number of vertices, and the large deviation theory of dense random graphs, which characterises the structure of rare events through constrained graphon optimisation. We represent graphons by implicit neural networks and optimise graphon objectives by gradient descent. Our design combines three ingredients: a multi-scale sinusoidal residual architecture biased toward sharp, step-like graphons; an embedded solver that enforces a single empirical density constraint and is differentiated by implicit differentiation; and symmetry-aware Monte Carlo estimators. On generalised Turán problems that previously required substantial human effort, our framework rediscovers known optimal graphons without human intervention. Applied to open instances, it produces candidate optima, including a previously unreported family of extremal structures. Applied to the variational problems from the large deviation theory of Erdős--Rényi random graphs, the framework produces new candidate optimal graphons across both upper- and lower-tail regimes for multiple pattern graphs; for the case of the triangle graph and the upper-tail regime, these candidates improve upon the best-known reference construction of Lubetzky and Zhao. The structures found by our framework have also led to new theorems on the optimal graphons for both families of problems.

entry.title: Conditional Flow Models for Offline Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
entry.summary: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits Hölder regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any Hölder index $β$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2β}{d+2β}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

entry.title: DBCM: Dual-Branch Calibration Module for Test-Time Adaptation in Time Series Forecasting
entry.summary: Non-stationarity induces test-time distribution shifts in time series forecasting (TSF), resulting in forecast residuals between predictions and the corresponding ground truth. Recent works on test-time adaptation for TSF address this by introducing lightweight calibration modules around frozen forecasters, updated using observations that become incrementally available at test time. Existing approaches typically employ channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming that forecast residuals are inherently channel-specific. However, we observe that forecast residuals often exhibit substantial shared structure across channels, suggesting that fully independent channel-wise parameterization may be redundant. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM), which shares adaptation capacity across channels through a shared adapter while retaining limited channel-specific flexibility through a low-rank channel-wise adapter, further enhanced by channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation. Extensive experiments show that DBCM consistently outperforms prior methods across diverse datasets, horizons, and backbones.

entry.title: Rethinking Representation Geometry in Supervised Contrastive Learning under Long-Tailed Data
entry.summary: Supervised contrastive learning and its balanced variants have demonstrated their effectiveness for representation learning under long-tailed distributions. However, although prior analyses suggest that their optimal representations may exhibit a regular simplex geometry, whether such a geometry is indeed exhibited remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a theoretical framework for these objectives that characterizes whether a regular simplex is formed at the optimum. By applying this to representative objectives, we show that these objectives fail to form a regular simplex at the optimum because they remain dependent on the number of samples per class. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce structural balancing that can be applied to contrastive objectives, and propose a fully balanced contrastive objective that provably forms a regular simplex geometry at its optimum. Both theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method yields a more balanced representation space and improves performance on long-tailed recognition and transfer learning tasks.

entry.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
entry.summary: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recently proposed extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We give a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error in terms of a residual component vanishing under compatibility. Next, we note that existing compatible objectives put density on velocities that are infeasible on compact manifolds. We propose an objective built from an exponential family over endpoints, with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. This manifests as a reweighting of the flow matching loss which, on constant-curvature manifolds, treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Empirically, our method recovers the correct velocity field on the test case, outperforms prior methods on high-dimensional product tori, and obtains substantial NLL improvements over prior work on two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere at moderate runtime overhead. On a large dataset of high-dimensional human poses, our method outperforms prior work according to sample-based metrics.

entry.title: Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference for Extending Trial Findings to Target Populations
entry.summary: The CODIACS Vanguard randomized trial compared a depression care intervention with usual care for patients with persistent depressive symptoms following acute coronary syndrome. We assess whether its findings can be extended to broader patient populations represented by two cohorts constructed from the All of Us electronic health records. This extension is challenging when treatment effects vary across covariates whose distributions differ between trial and target populations. We develop Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference (PSPI), an interaction-based outcome modeling framework that combines Bayesian additive regression trees for potentially high-dimensional covariates with natural cubic splines of the sampling propensity score. Two variants include a separate spline in the treatment effect component alone or in both the prognostic and treatment effect components. The spline components allow separate regularization of selection-related variation and thus improve potential outcome estimation within the observed range and allow an explicit extrapolation rule beyond their boundary knots under substantial covariate shift. An inverse Gumbel transformation of the sampling propensity score balances compression near zero and the extent of extrapolation. Simulation studies show that spline-based PSPI models outperform competing methods in the settings studied, achieving lower root mean squared errors and near-nominal coverage, particularly under substantial covariate shift. In the application, PSPI estimates larger intervention benefits in both target populations than the unadjusted trial estimate.

entry.title: Combinatorial Characterizations of the Learnability of Conditional Distributions
entry.summary: We study the PAC-learnability of function classes that map inputs to probability distributions over a finite space. The learner observes i.i.d. input-label pairs, with each label sampled from the conditional distribution of an unknown target hypothesis in the class. We measure learning through excess risk under a bounded proper loss that satisfies two mild assumptions. We introduce the \textbf{fat$_γ$Natarajan dimension}, which generalizes both fat$_γ$ and Natarajan dimension, and prove that its finiteness at every positive scale is necessary and sufficient for learnability. We also introduce a \textbf{fat$_γ$Graph} dimension extending the classical \gra dimension and establish inequalities comparing the two dimensions at different scales, leading to an equivalent characterization of learnability. Finally, we show that a distribution-valued function class is learnable if and only if each of its coordinate classes is learnable in the probabilistic concept model.

entry.title: Early learning in large residual networks
entry.summary: We study the early training dynamics of nonlinear residual networks with blocks of zero hidden layers as a model of more general residual networks. We analyze networks in a sequential limit where first width and depth diverge, then the number of training data points diverges, and finally the input dimension diverges. This is a more refined setup compared to the typical mean-field theory analysis in which depth and width diverge but the number of training datapoints and input dimension are fixed. Our main technical result is a diagrammatic computation of both the network output and the hidden representations after the few steps of gradient descent in terms of the statistics of inner products of inputs from the training set. One of our principle conceptual findings is a negative result: in the limit of large input dimension the network output can learn only a linear function of its inputs early in training since higher learned monomials are more and more suppressed in the input dimension and vanish in the large dimension limit. This suggests that mean-field limits of ResNets are surprisingly rigid in the regime of high input dimension and may not be sufficient toy models for understanding feature learning. Finally, we investigate how to ensure hyperparameter transfer for the learning rate as a function of dataset size and input dimension. We test our predictions numerically and find excellent agreement with our theory.

entry.title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
entry.summary: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent $α>1$ and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared $L_2$ approximation rate $\mathcal{O}((κ_P\log(m/δ)/m)^α)$ for two-layer networks of width $m$ and trainable proportion $P$, where $κ_P=(P/κ_1^*+(1-P)/κ_0^*)^{-1}$. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least $1-δ$. The constants $κ_0^*$ and $κ_1^*$ quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension $d$, we verify these assumptions with $α=(d+2)/(d-1)$ and $κ_0^*=4\sqrt{2}τ(d+1)/d$ for initialization scale $τ\ge1$, and $κ_1^*=1$ under ridge leverage sampling. For $d=5$ and $τ=10$, a trainable proportion of approximately $4.1\%$ captures $90\%$ of the reduction in the approximation bound from $P=0$ to $P=1$. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.

entry.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
entry.summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

entry.title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
entry.summary: The attention mechanism underpins modern large language models, yet their dynamics remain only partially understood. Recent perspectives interpret attention blocks as interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limits correspond to gradient flows of energy functionals on spaces of probability densities on $\mathbb R^d$ equipped with Wasserstein-type metrics. We extend this viewpoint by deriving accelerated attention blocks from inertial, Nesterov-type damped Hamiltonian dynamics on these density spaces, developing the geometry and differential calculus needed to make the construction rigorous. In particular, we introduce a local-mobility geometry for the Otto-Wasserstein and softmax-Wasserstein settings, and a quotient Stein geometry that resolves the degeneracy of the linear-attention kernel to yield a well-defined metric and differential calculus. We provide rigorous foundations when softmax attention admits a gradient-flow formulation and when its inertial counterpart admits a damped Hamiltonian on explicitly characterized domains. For linear attention, we obtain a finite-dimensional solution theory with sharp conditions for global existence versus finite-time second-moment blow-up. We further prove a quantitative link between continuous moment blow-up and the discrete-layer depth at which token norms cross a prescribed threshold. Finally, motivated by the finite-token geometry, we propose geometric corrections to token and momentum updates. In decoder-only, nanoGPT-style experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText, these corrections lower validation negative log-likelihood on next-token prediction relative to momentum-only controls.

entry.title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
entry.summary: Online Policy Distillation (OPD) often outperforms offline methods such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) by training on trajectories sampled directly from the student. However, standard OPD trains the student to follow the teacher at every state of the trajectory, assuming that teacher guidance is always beneficial. We instead distinguish between what the teacher prefers and what actually helps the current student succeed. We introduce Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation (AOPD), which weights teacher actions by their counterfactual advantage under the student. Teacher actions that improve the student's expected outcome are reinforced, while those that do not are downweighted. Directly computing these advantages requires trying alternative teacher actions at each step and running new rollouts from each. Instead, we show that the AOPD objective can be estimated using only standard student rollouts and their terminal rewards. Our estimator uses teacher importance weights on the student-sampled actions to provide unbiased advantage-weighted supervision, without any additional rollouts or reward evaluations. This allows AOPD to focus teacher supervision on actions that help the current student while preserving the rollout efficiency of standard OPD. Experiments on math, coding, and Medqa show gains over distillation and RL baselines in both external-teacher and self-distillation settings.

entry.title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks
entry.summary: \emph{Continuous-space} attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs by sampling or optimizing over a low-dimensional Gaussian latent space and decoding it to text through a \emph{random mapping} and nearest-token lookup. Because the random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural, and as such easily detectable through input guardrails, and the risk estimates they yield are not grounded in natural prompts. In this paper, we demonstrate that the same continuous latent-space framework can be coupled directly to a learned generative distribution over language, a continuous diffusion language model (dLLM), which removes the artificial random mapping while preserving the standard-Gaussian latent formulation and the downstream sampling or optimization procedure. We evaluate this approach under two settings: sampling-based estimation using \emph{RareTrap} and optimization-based search using \emph{ThinkTrap}. We find that character-level perplexity drops from $10^3$--$10^7$ to 3--5 in RareTrap and from 20--28 to 4.3--5.4 in ThinkTrap. We also find that model risk estimates can differ by an order of magnitude across the two mappings.

entry.title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting
entry.summary: Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

entry.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
entry.summary: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.

entry.title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
entry.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention-based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal-criterion sensitivity ($\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$) proposed by~\citep{guan2025monitoring}. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish $\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$ as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control--intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention-specific training methods based on off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyue-lxy/learning-to-be-monitored.

entry.title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
entry.summary: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

entry.title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
entry.summary: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

entry.title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
entry.summary: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

entry.title: Local Discrimination of Binary Classifiers via Localized AUC Functional
entry.summary: Risk prediction models are frequently evaluated with AUC, which means that during evaluation we are blind to performance heterogeneity, which could lead to bad decision-making in clinics. In this work, we aim to change that by identifying patient cohorts for whom the risk prediction model might not be an accurate predictor. To separate these cohorts, we use a version of the weighted AUC, which we call Localized AUC or LAUC. Using this metric, we build a method that we coin LOCATOR. This method is able to identify cohorts of patients for whom the risk prediction model is inaccurate. We test this method both in real-world data and in simulations. We also build a statistical background for the use of Localized AUC for our purposes.

entry.title: Operationalising Weaker Faithfulness: Recovery, Ambiguity and Computational Limits
entry.summary: Variables can predict an outcome jointly while each is individually independent of it, causing structure learners to discard informative links. We investigate how to operationalise weaker faithfulness through two approaches: selective protection in an adjacency learner and explicit retention of alternative directed graph explanations. Matched experiments show that changes at both an early candidate-removal stage and later pruning can be necessary. In noisy XOR with a descendant (N = 10,000, 20 matched samples), combining reactivation and protection raises complete parent-pair recovery from 0/20 for either change alone to 20/20, while adding false edges. A confirmation study shows that the family estimator can preserve explanations lost by orienting the protected learner's selected skeleton: in one weaker signal XOR condition (N = 10,000) it retains the entire reference family in 48/50 samples, compared with 0/50 for the skeleton adapter. These gains are conditional. Protection can add only error, weaker effects produce false exclusions, and an ordinary faithful-chain comparison favours the PC learner. Complete nonempty family outputs decline at six/eight variables, and all 400 twelve/twenty-variable searches remain unfinished at the reporting cutoff. Neural controls show engineered retention, while the family estimator returns no accepted graph within its application budget. This operationalisation identifies two deletion stages that must be coordinated in the motivating example and shows when direct family search preserves explanations lost by selecting one skeleton. Finite evidence and computation remain substantial barriers to reliable general inference.

entry.title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
entry.summary: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

entry.title: What Comes Next and Why: Interpretable Next-Event Prediction with Neuro-Symbolic Rules
entry.summary: In real-world applications, being able to explain why a prediction is made is often as important - if not more so - than achieving high accuracy. However, existing methods for sequential event prediction typically prioritize accuracy at the expense of interpretability. Neuro-symbolic approaches offer a promising direction to improve interpretability by learning symbolic rules, but extending them to next-event prediction is challenging due to the presence of temporal dependencies. We introduce RULES, a neuro-symbolic model that learns sequential rules directly from data, and combine it with a residual network to form RUNES (Rule Network for Event Sequences). RULES accurately recovers ground truth rules from synthetic data and discovers compact, interpretable rule sets on real data. RUNES combines these rules additively with a residual network, achieving competitive accuracy while providing transparent access to active rules and how residuals adjust predictions.

entry.title: Transformers with CoT Discover Heavy-Ball Acceleration Through Training
entry.summary: Modern transformers often solve complex tasks by generating and refining intermediate reasoning steps. To develop a theoretical understanding of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, a notable recent study by Huang et al. (2025) viewed transformers as algorithm executors, and showed that when transformers' CoT steps are supervised by a gradient-descent teacher, they can learn to implement gradient descent for in-context weight prediction in linear regression. In this paper, we study the same in-context weight prediction task but ask whether CoT reasoning can go beyond merely imitating the teacher algorithm. We show that, after initial supervision from a gradient-descent teacher, further trajectory-level supervision using the true regression weights leads the model to implement the Heavy-Ball method, thereby achieving acceleration over the original teacher. Notably, this accelerated algorithm emerges without supervision from any Heavy-Ball teacher. Our results provide a concrete theoretical example in which transformer reasoning can discover new algorithms through training, rather than merely imitate the algorithm used for supervision.

entry.title: Random Projections for Spectral Algorithms: Optimal Rates in Sobolev Norms
entry.summary: Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nyström sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> α_0-1/β$, where $s,β$, and $α_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $α_0=1/β$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2τ]$ with $τ$ and $γ$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

entry.title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
entry.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

entry.title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
entry.summary: Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.

entry.title: Width and Depth Limits Commute During Training
entry.summary: Recent work established that the infinite-width and infinite-depth limits of residual networks commute at initialization when residual branches are scaled by $1/\sqrt{depth}$. In particular, the network output converges to the same limit whether width and depth tend to infinity sequentially or jointly. We extend this commutativity result to training in linear residual networks. Under the same $1/\sqrt{depth}$ residual-branch scaling (Depth-$μ$P) and the $μ$P width parameterization, we prove that, for any fixed number of gradient-descent steps with gradient clipping, the network output converges in $L^2$ along every joint width--depth growth path as both width and depth tend to infinity. Consequently, the infinite-width and infinite-depth limits commute throughout any finite training horizon. Without gradient clipping, the corresponding $L^2$ convergence does not hold in general, but we establish the weaker convergence in probability.

entry.title: Residual Calibration via Local Feature-Space Refinement
entry.summary: Deep neural networks often struggle to provide reliable confidence estimates, making post-hoc calibration essential for reliable decision-making. Existing post-hoc methods largely rely on score-based transformations, which improve marginal calibration but often fail to capture spatially varying miscalibration in local regions of the learned feature space. To address this gap, we propose Local Adaptive Probability Estimation (LAPE), a post-hoc residual calibration framework. Specifically, LAPE treats the global calibrator output as a stable anchor and refines the individual prediction by leveraging non-parametric local evidence from neighboring calibration samples. As a plug-and-play refinement module, LAPE effectively utilizes the information about feature-space geometry and can reuse the calibration data that are used to construct the global calibrator. Furthermore, we extend LAPE to the setting with multi-view inputs through Cascade Feature Augmentation Fusion (CFAF). Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed methods can improve the calibration quality of various existing baselines and remain efficient and robust across different settings.

entry.title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
entry.summary: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.

entry.title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
entry.summary: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.

entry.title: High-Value Training Data from Noisy, Diverse Sources
entry.summary: Training state-of-the-art models increasingly requires learning from large, heterogeneous datasets whose examples vary in quality, domain relevance, and source of supervision. Dataweighting---assigning different weights to training examples---offers a general way to control how such data influences training, but learning effective weights at scale remains challenging. We develop a scalable approach to learning dataweights: given a small, high-quality target dataset, we use metagradients through the training process to efficiently optimize training-example weights directly for performance on the target domain. To scale beyond a fixed dataset and model, we learn parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from smaller models to substantially larger ones. We study reward modeling as a prototypical application, where preference data may be noisy, adversarial, synthetic, or mismatched with the target domain. Learned dataweights improve held-out performance, automatically adapt reward models to specialized domains, and allow mixtures of human and synthetic supervision to outperform either source alone.
